_comment: Seed concepts for synthetic ARC puzzle generation. 'target' seeds describe rule FAMILIES that NVARC misses on the public eval set (multi-step, object-relational, many-colour tasks). 'broad' seeds keep coverage wide so the model does not over-fit to one style. Descriptions are written at the family level; none copies a specific ARC task.

seeds.description: Several objects stand on or hang from each other. Apply gravity or a push in one direction, but objects move only when nothing supports them; the order in which they move matters (an object cannot pass through another). Output is the settled configuration.

Straight lines of different colours cross each other. A rule decides which colour is drawn on top at crossings (for example: the colour whose line is longer, or whose endpoint marker is a specific colour, or horizontal always over vertical). Input shows lines with crossings missing or wrong; output shows them resolved.

Each object contains or touches a number of small marker cells. The number of markers decides what happens to the object: its new colour, whether it is deleted, how far it moves, or how many times it is repeated.

Closed frames (rectangles or irregular outlines) contain zero or more smaller objects. The relationship (inside / outside / touching the border / how many inside) determines the transformation: recolour the frame, fill it, move the contents, or remove the frame.
A regular repeating or symmetric pattern is partly covered by a blob of one colour (noise or an occluder). The output restores the hidden cells using the pattern, or outputs only the restored patch.

A rule with two independent steps that must both be applied: first extract or select a region (for example the object with the most cells, or the panel marked by a special cell), then apply a transform to it (rotate, recolour by legend, scale) before output.

The grid is split by separator lines into blocks of equal size. Output reorders, stacks, transposes or interleaves the blocks according to a property of each block (count of coloured cells, presence of a marker, colour), possibly changing the overall layout from horizontal to vertical.

Hollow shapes each carry one marker cell of a different colour somewhere on or near their border. Fill each shape's interior with its marker colour, remove the marker, or extend the marker colour along the shape's border.

The input shows the first few frames of a process arranged as panels (growth, rotation, movement, counting). Output is the next frame or the completed sequence, or the whole sequence folded into a single panel.

Objects come in pairs related by shape (same shape, mirror image, or one is the hole of the other) but different colours or positions. Pair them and act on the pair: move one onto the other, recolour the partner, or draw a connector between them.

A large shape has a symmetry (mirror, 4-fold, rotational) but several cells are corrupted or missing. Output completes the symmetry, or outputs only the corrupted cells, or marks them with a new colour.
A path starts at a marked cell and travels in a direction. It turns, bounces, or changes colour when it hits obstacles of specific colours, or stops at a target. Output draws the full path.

Six or more colours are present. A small legend or key region maps colours to actions or to other colours; the rest of the grid must be transformed by looking up each object's colour in the legend (recolour, delete, mirror, move by k cells).
Scattered single-cell noise of one colour is sprinkled over a scene. The noise must be removed and a second rule applied to the clean scene (connect objects, fill enclosed areas, or outline shapes).

Several objects of one colour differ in size. Rank them (largest to smallest, or by width, by number of holes) and recolour each by its rank using a fixed palette, or keep only the k-th largest, or sort them into a row.

Cells of the same colour that share a row or column are connected by a line of that colour. Where lines of different colours would intersect, a rule decides the intersection cell (a third colour, the earlier colour, or leave a gap).

The grid is a grid of cells (an n-by-n arrangement of small sub-grids separated by lines). The output is a small grid with one cell per sub-grid summarising it (majority colour, is-it-symmetric, count parity), or the reverse: expand a small grid into a meta-grid.

Each object carries a flag cell (a differently coloured cell at one corner). The flag's position or colour determines the transform applied to that object alone: rotate 90, mirror horizontally, shift, or scale by 2.
The output size depends on a count in the input: the number of objects, of distinct colours, or of marker cells sets how many times a template is repeated or how large it is drawn.

Three or more equal panels separated by lines. Output is one panel computed by a Boolean or voting rule across panels (cell is set where an odd number of panels have it, where all have it, where exactly one has it, or the majority colour).

An object moves in a direction until it hits a wall or another object, then stops, merges, bounces, or leaves a trail. Several objects may move in different directions indicated by an arrow-like cell.
A large shape has holes of different shapes; loose pieces elsewhere match the holes. Move each piece into the hole it fits (allowing rotation), or recolour the hole with the piece's colour.
Treat each object's border cells and interior cells differently: swap their colours, recolour the border by the count of interior cells, or grow the border outward by one cell in a new colour.

A reference object (unique colour or shape) sits somewhere in the grid. Every other object is transformed according to where it lies relative to the reference: above, below, left, right, or diagonal (recolour by direction, or move toward it until touching).

Output is a crop of the input chosen by a rule that needs comparison across candidates: the rectangle with the most distinct colours, the only non-symmetric block, the object whose colour appears exactly once, or the region enclosed by a specific colour.
Recolour each object according to a simple property: its size, whether it touches the grid edge, whether it is a rectangle, or how many cells it has.
Fill enclosed empty regions inside closed shapes with a given colour; regions open to the edge stay empty. Variants: fill colour depends on region size.
Mirror the grid or an object across an axis given by a line of cells, producing a symmetric output that may be larger than the input.
Tile a small input pattern into a larger output with a rule for alternate tiles (flip, rotate, recolour).
From each coloured cell draw a line in a direction given by its colour (or until an obstacle); lines may be horizontal, vertical or diagonal.
Extract a single object from a cluttered grid by a simple criterion (largest, smallest, unique colour) and output its bounding box.
Scale the grid up or down by an integer factor; when scaling down, each block maps to one cell by majority or by a specified position.
Replace each solid object by its outline, or add an outline of a new colour around each object, or draw its bounding box.
Move all objects of one colour to a specified edge, keeping their order, while other objects stay fixed.
Output a small grid encoding a count: one cell per object, or a bar whose length equals the number of objects of each colour, sorted.
Swap two colours everywhere, or cycle colours according to a mapping shown by a pair of example cells in the input.
Draw concentric rings around a seed cell, with colours cycling in a fixed order until the grid edge or an obstacle is reached.
Rotate every object 90 degrees about its own centre, or rotate the whole grid, with a marker indicating the direction.
Repeat an object in a direction with a fixed gap until the grid edge, possibly shrinking or recolouring on each repetition.
Find the largest all-empty rectangle (or the largest solid rectangle) and fill or mark it.
